fields.title: Test before building
fields.keyTakeaway: The most expensive test is to build and see. A prototype answers whether users will understand, while shutting down an existing feature answers whether it is needed, and both take days rather than months.
fields.checkQuestion: How do you test the value of a feature that does not exist yet without building it?
fields.blocks/0/text: The same question about an experiment, but for the stage **when there is nothing to build yet or it is too expensive.**
fields.blocks/1/subtitle: Tests understanding and intent, but not value
fields.blocks/1/items/0: **What you learn:** whether the scenario is clear, whether people find what they need, what they expect to see next.
fields.blocks/1/items/1: **What you won't learn:** whether they will use it regularly or pay. Words about the future remain words.
fields.blocks/1/items/2: Cheapest of all — a clickable mockup and five people; this is enough to find major understanding issues.
fields.blocks/2/subtitle: Turn off what already exists and see if people notice
fields.blocks/2/items/0: Works where people debate the value of an existing feature.
fields.blocks/2/items/1: **How:** disable for a small fraction of users for a limited period.
fields.blocks/2/items/2: **What to look at:** support tickets, churn, behavior — not a survey.
fields.blocks/2/items/3: The only way to distinguish “used because it's there” from “actually needed”.
fields.blocks/3/text:
For six months, they debated whether to invest in downloading books for offline reading. Data showed that 6% of users used the feature — low, but advocates argued these were the most loyal users.

They disabled offline for 2% of users for two weeks. Support tickets — 34, all from people who read on the subway. Churn in this group grew threefold over two weeks.

The 6% turned out not to be a small fraction, but a high-value segment. The issue was closed in two weeks instead of another quarter of debates.
fields.blocks/4/text: A Deprivation test degrades the product for real people. A small segment, a short duration, the ability to roll back immediately, and readiness to explain are mandatory.
fields.blocks/4/title: Shut off carefully and for a short time
fields.blocks/5/text: A prototype overestimates intent: people are polite and say they will use it. Deprivation testing is inapplicable where the cost of error is high — payments, security, legally binding actions. And both methods answer “is it needed”, but not “how much will it bring”.
